title: US Intel Warns Iran Assassination Plots Against Officials at Advanced Stages
excerpt: A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel, prompting embassy staff reductions across the Middle East.
body:
• US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on October 23 that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target American diplomats and officials, with lethal plots at advanced stages.
  • The State Department has ordered family members and nonessential staff out of Saudi Arabia and reduced personnel at embassies in the UAE, Lebanon, Qatar and Jordan.
  • Clayton offered to downgrade intelligence so warnings can reach personnel without security clearances who may be at risk.
  • President Donald Trump said Friday the US may launch another Operation Epic Fury unless Iran agrees to a deal.

United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran has significantly escalated efforts to assassinate American diplomats and government officials overseas, with some plots reaching advanced stages, according to a memorandum obtained by Axios and reported by the Associated Press via Newsmax. India Today also reported the warning as the Middle East war escalates.

The one-page, unclassified memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, sent on Friday, October 23, says agencies identified a substantial increase in Iranian efforts to target US personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere. It does not identify specific targets, countries outside the Middle East where attacks might occur, or details of the suspected plots, but says senior State Department officials have already received the underlying intelligence. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.

Warnings to reach staff without clearances

Clayton warned that intelligence about the plots must be shared more broadly with American personnel who could be in danger, including those not currently authorized to receive it. He offered to downgrade the classification of as much intelligence as possible so the State Department can distribute warnings widely and quickly.

"We decided that due to the threat of Houthi attacks and Iranian terror plots we need to reduce our footprint and keep only essential staff."

— US official, speaking to Axios

Embassy drawdowns across the region

The threat has already changed staffing. Earlier this week the State Department ordered family members and nonessential personnel to leave the US Embassy in Riyadh and consulates in Jeddah and Dhahran in Saudi Arabia. On Friday it also ordered reductions at embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar and Jordan, according to a US official cited by Axios; CNN first reported the additional reductions. Officials also worry Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen could expand attacks beyond Saudi Arabia to other countries in the region.

Stalled talks and a threat of renewed strikes

The warning comes as efforts to negotiate an end to the war remain stalled. The United States and Iran held talks during the UN General Assembly in September but stayed divided over terms. Speaking at a rally in Florida on Friday, President Donald Trump suggested Tehran could face another American operation unless it agrees to a deal.

"We may do another little Operation Epic Fury, or [the Iranians] will agree [to a deal]."

— President Donald Trump

Earlier this month, Trump administration officials held high-level discussions about resuming major combat operations against Iran, Axios previously reported. For Indian nationals and diaspora families with relatives working in Gulf states, the embassy drawdowns and the Houthi threat are a reminder to follow local advisories closely, though the memo names no threat to Indian personnel.

What happens next

The State Department has not commented publicly on the specific plots. Whether Washington resumes strikes, and whether Tehran signals willingness to negotiate, will shape the security calculus in coming days, with US missions in the region operating on essential staff only in the meantime.
